title: How Computer Automation Affects Occupations: Technology, Jobs, and Skills
pub: Boston University School of Law, Law & Economics Working Paper No. 15-49
author: James Bessen

st.t: Job exposure: Which tasks vanish changes outcomes
st.an: Bessen accepts that task automation does not mechanically eliminate occupations and materially develops the proposition with evidence that demand expansion and inter-occupation substitution can produce near-zero aggregate employment effects while redistributing outcomes across occupations, wages and skill levels. His occupation-specific learning mechanism further explains how aggregate resilience can coexist with greater within-occupation inequality.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Bessen supports the cluster’s core claim that automation primarily reallocates work and changes skill demand rather than mechanically eliminating occupations. He materially extends it with historical occupational evidence and a demand-side mechanism showing why task automation can increase or decrease employment. However, the paper predates generative legal AI and does not address jagged capability, verification or legal operating-model design directly.

st.t: Employment effects: Task substitution permits stable jobs
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: automation changes particular tasks within occupational bundles, while employment outcomes depend conditionally on demand growth, substitution and occupational structure rather than following mechanically from productivity gains. Its warning that future automation may still reduce labor demand is a caveat already consistent with the synthesis, not opposition.

Because of these indivisibilities, firms hire workers to perform a bundle of interrelated tasks rather than having them specialize in a single task.

kp.k: Study tracks detailed US occupations through 2013
kp.d: Bessen analyses a balanced panel of 317 consistent US occupations using Census data for 1980, 1990 and 2000 and American Community Survey data for 2013. Computer use is measured from October Current Population Survey supplements in 1984, 1989, 1993 and 1997; the paper notes that its analysis concerns computer automation rather than every form of digital technological change.
qs: I estimate the model for a consistent set of detailed occupations from 1980 through 2013.
My resulting panel had 317 consistent occupations populated in each year studied.
Computer use data come from a supplement to the October Current Population Surveys (CPS) of 1984, 1989, 1993, and 1997, which asked whether adult respondents directly used a computer at work.
In another respect, this analysis is limited: it only concerns computer automation, not the entire range of computer-related technological change.

kp.k: Computer-using occupations grew faster, not slower
kp.d: The empirical analysis associates greater occupational computer use with faster employment growth rather than direct job elimination. The summary reports approximately 0.9% additional annual employment growth at mean computer use; depending on specification, Table 2 reports contributions from 0.47% to 1.29% per year for the full sample.
qs: Occupations that use computers grow faster, not slower.
At the sample mean, computer use is associated with about a 0.9% increase in employment per year.
Overall, computer use is associated with employment growth that is nearly 1 percent per annum faster at the sample mean, both for routine and mid-wage occupations and for the entire sample.

kp.d: The full model finds two countervailing associations: computer use within an occupation is linked to faster growth, while computer use by other occupations in the same industry is linked to substitution away from the focal occupation. At sample means these effects yield a negligible estimated net employment effect of -0.07% per year, which the paper reports as neither economically nor statistically different from zero.
qs: Overall, inter-occupation substitution offsets the growth effect so that the net effect of computer use on total employment is negligible (-.07% per year).

The two effects roughly cancel each other out: while computer use by workers in an occupation is associated with faster job growth, workers in other occupations within the industry tend to substitute for the subject occupation when they use computers.
The net combined effect of computer use is neither economically nor statistically different from zero.

kp.k: Automation reallocated work toward higher-paid occupations
kp.d: Because computer adoption was heavier in higher-wage occupations, substitution was uneven. The full-model estimates associate computer use with a statistically significant net decline for low-wage occupations and statistically significant net growth for high-wage occupations, implying displacement and occupational transition rather than aggregate technological unemployment.
qs: However, because higher wage occupations use computers more, computer use tends to increase well-paid jobs and to decrease low-paid jobs.

These findings suggest that while computer use has little effect on the total number of jobs, the substitution effect is associated with a substantial transfer of work from low- paying occupations that do not use computers much to higher paying occupations that use computers more.

Computer use does not contribute to economic inequality by causing technological unemployment. But computers might contribute to economic inequality if it is costly or difficult for workers to acquire new skills in order to transition into growing occupations.

kp.k: Routine and mid-wage occupations also grew directly
kp.d: Contrary to claims that computer automation directly eliminates routine or mid-wage work and thereby produces job polarization, occupational computer use was associated with faster direct growth in both groups. Once inter-occupation substitution was included, routine-intensive occupations showed a modest net decline, but that estimate was not statistically significant.
qs: This association is true in general and also for occupations that perform more routine tasks and for mid-wage occupations.
Instead, computer use is associated with substantially faster growth of an occupation.
Column 3 looks again at routine intensive occupations and finds, in contrast to Table 2, a modest net decline, although this estimate is not statistically significant.

kp.k: Adoption followed payoffs more than task routineness
kp.d: Although routine tasks were associated with computer use, abstract-task importance, occupational wages, education and occupation size were stronger correlates. The relationship between routine-task importance and adoption also weakened over time, leading Bessen to argue that economic returns to automating well-paid occupations were more important determinants of adoption.
qs: While the importance of routine tasks to an occupation is associated with greater computer use, the importance of abstract tasks is much more significant.
Occupations with more routine tasks have slower growth in computer use than others; occupations where abstract tasks are more important have faster growth in computer use.
In summary, the extent to which occupations perform routine tasks is not a very important factor in determining computer use and the significance of this factor appears to have diminished over time.
The importance of the economic payoff to automation seems to be a much more important driver of endogenous adoption decisions and the payoff appears to be greater in well-paid occupations.

kp.k: Computer use widened within-occupation wage inequality
kp.d: Computer use was significantly associated with growth in both the 90/50 and 50/10 wage gaps within occupations. A counterfactual based on 1990-2013 estimates attributes about 40% of the workforce-wide increase in the 90/50 gap and 32% of the increase in the 50/10 gap to computer use; the paper interprets this as consistent with costly acquisition of occupation-specific skills rather than technological unemployment.
qs: Computer use is also associated with greater inequality of wages within occupations.

This association contributes to wage inequality, accounting for 40% of the growth in the wage gap between the 90th and 50th percentiles of the entire workforce since 1990; it can account for 32% of the increase in the 50/10 wage gap.
This greater disparity appears to arise from a growing demand for skills, particularly occupation-specific skills that might be costly to acquire.

kp.k: Computerization increased demand for college-educated workers
kp.d: Computer use was associated with an increased share of workers having at least four years of post-secondary education, including in occupations with few abstract tasks or where college credentials were generally not required. The association between rising college shares and wage growth in computer-using occupations is presented as evidence against oversupply of college graduates being the main explanation.
qs: Computer use is associated with an increase in the share of an occupation’s workforce with four or more years of college, even for occupations that do not require a college degree.
Both columns show a significant positive association between computer use and growth in the college share of workers.
The growth in the college share is strongly associated with wage growth in occupations that use computers, suggesting that an oversupply of college graduates is not a major factor.

kp.k: Legal support employment grew despite e-discovery
kp.d: As a legal-sector example within the broader occupational study, the paper reports that electronic discovery software expanded rapidly while employment among legal assistants, paralegals and legal support occupations continued to grow. From 2000 through 2013, these occupations grew 1.1% annually in full-time-equivalent terms, faster than the workforce, despite both e-discovery and substantial offshoring.
qs: Since the late 1990s, electronic document discovery software for legal proceedings has grown into a billion dollar business doing work done by paralegals, but the number of paralegals has grown robustly.

From 2000 through 2013, fulltime equivalent jobs for legal assistants, paralegals, and legal support occupations grew 1.1% per year, faster than the workforce. This growth occurred despite substantial offshoring as well.

kp.k: Automation changes tasks and occupation-specific skills
kp.d: The paper distinguishes automation of tasks from elimination of entire occupations. Its model allows automation to lower costs, expand product demand and increase an occupation's efficiency relative to other occupations. The bank-teller example illustrates employment growth alongside a shift from routine cash handling toward marketing and interpersonal skills, while the broader findings emphasize new jobs, new workflows and occupation-specific learning.
qs: The distinction between tasks and occupations is important because conclusions about tasks do not translate unambiguously into conclusions about occupations, as the example of the bank tellers shows.
New technology can increase demand for an occupation, offsetting putative job losses.
At the same time, teller skills changed. Non-routine marketing and interpersonal skills became more valuable, while routine cash handling became less important.
Workers need to learn new jobs and new ways of working.

kp.d: Bessen cautions that the estimates may not capture digital technology's role in offshoring, consumer self-service, transfers between industries or other extra-industry organizational changes. Computer use is also only a proxy for labor augmentation, and instrumental-variable estimation may not resolve every causal concern.
qs: Instrumental variables estimation might not address all concerns about causality.
Also, computer automation might be poorly measured.
Moreover, this study only measures the use of computers within an industry.

Digital technology appears to play some role in extra-industry changes: digital technology might facilitate transfer of work offshore, or to consumers in the form of self-service (e.g., airline ticket kiosks), or from one industry to another.

kp.k: Future automation may eventually reduce employment
kp.d: The historical findings are not presented as a guarantee about future technology. Bessen predicts conditionally that employment effects may worsen as high-growth applications are exhausted or demand becomes saturated, drawing an analogy to nineteenth-century textile weaving, where automation initially accompanied employment growth but later stable employment and decline.
qs: However, there is no guarantee that future computer technology will increase labor demand.
If history is a guide, computers may eventually tend to reduce the number of jobs as more marginal computer applications are exploited that do not produce as much job growth.
Eventually, however, demand became more saturated and further technical improvements were accompanied by stable employment and then decline.

kp.k: Workforce challenge is learning, not unemployment
kp.d: The paper's concluding argument is that the principal contemporary problem is costly skill formation and occupational transition, not major net technological unemployment. Because the required capabilities include occupation-specific and organizational knowledge beyond formal education, Bessen argues that simply increasing college graduation rates will not meet the challenge.
qs: Thus although computers are not cause major technological unemployment, the development of new skills is nevertheless a major challenge to the workforce.
Yet these skills involve much that is different from what is taught in college. The challenge will not be met simply by increasing college graduation rates.
Nevertheless, the technological challenge facing today’s workforce is not unemployment but a difficulty learning the skills needed to use new technology.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Bessen argues that computer automation historically increased employment in computer-using occupations while displacing work in other occupations, with little net employment effect; its principal challenges were changing skills and wage inequality.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain study of computer automation, not a study of contemporary generative AI. Bessen reports that computer use is associated with approximately 0.9 percentage points faster annual occupational employment growth at the sample mean, including in routine and mid-wage occupations. Once substitution between occupations within industries is included, the estimated aggregate contribution is negligible, at -0.07 percentage points annually. He argues that this pattern does not support computer automation as a substantial source of technological unemployment or job polarization during the study period. Instead, employment shifts from low-paid, less-computerized occupations toward higher-paid, more-computerized occupations. Computer use is also associated with greater within-occupation wage dispersion and rising shares of college-educated workers, including where degrees are not required. His proposed explanation emphasizes costly acquisition of occupation-specific skills. The directly legal example is electronic discovery: software performed work previously done by paralegals while legal-support employment continued growing. He does not predict that future automation must preserve this employment pattern.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on occupational employment and wage regressions, a theoretical model of task automation and occupational substitution, and historical examples.
pts.d: Bessen analyzes 317 consistently defined US occupations using 1% Census samples for 1980, 1990 and 2000 and the 2013 American Community Survey. Computer use is measured from the 1984, 1989, 1993 and 1997 CPS supplements; their occupational averages correlate 0.88 with the 2013 O*NET measure of interacting with computers. His full-model baseline covers 10,837 occupation-industry cells. He reports weighted regressions, instrumental-variable estimates, controls for occupational and industry groups, and robustness checks addressing selection, outliers and occupational definitions. The wage counterfactual attributes approximately 40% of the 1990–2013 increase in the workforce-wide 90/50 wage gap and 32% of the 50/10 increase to the estimated association with computer use; these are model-based accounting exercises, not experimentally established causal shares. The legal example reports 1.1% annual full-time-equivalent growth in legal assistants, paralegals and legal-support occupations during 2000–2013, despite electronic discovery and offshoring. Other illustrations include ATMs and tellers, barcode scanners and cashiers, and historical textile weaving. Bessen expressly acknowledges remaining causal and measurement limitations.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The principal findings concern 1980–2013; Bessen explicitly makes future employment outcomes conditional on demand, substitution and the scope of automation.
pts.d: The paper was published in November 2015. Employment and skill-upgrading estimates principally concern 1980–2013, the cited legal-support growth concerns 2000–2013, and the wage-inequality counterfactual concerns 1990–2013. The theoretical model permits either employment growth or decline: reduced costs can expand product demand, and more productive occupations can substitute for other occupations. Outcomes depend on product-demand elasticity, occupational substitutability and the occupation's wage-bill share. The model principally concerns automation of tasks within occupations rather than complete automation of all their tasks. Empirical coverage is limited to computer use within industries, not the entire range of digitally enabled organizational changes, offshore transfers or self-service. Bessen warns that future applications may generate less demand growth and eventually reduce employment as markets become saturated. He presents this as a possibility, without a dated forecast. His skills explanation depends on new capabilities being costly or difficult to acquire; increasing college graduation alone is not sufficient.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are workers across US occupations, with uneven consequences by computer adoption, wage level and ability to acquire new skills; legal-support workers provide one specific illustration.
pts.d: The empirical population consists of civilian wage-and-salary workers aged 16–64 in the 50 US states, excluding self-employed workers, unpaid family workers and institutional residents. More-computerized, higher-wage occupations tend to gain work, while less-computerized, lower-wage occupations face displacement through substitution. Routine and mid-wage occupations show positive direct associations with computer use, but their estimated net effects after substitution are modestly negative and statistically insignificant. Within occupations, workers able to acquire new technology-specific skills may gain relative to those who cannot, widening wage disparities. Workers moving between occupations face retraining costs, and employers face organizational change and demand for new capabilities. In legal services, the concrete affected group is legal assistants, paralegals and other legal-support workers whose aggregate employment grew while electronic discovery automated some work. The paper does not establish separate effects on law-firm staffing structures, legal pricing, clients or access to justice.
